candidates.headline: Musixmatch gave 1.5 million artists a wallet for their lyric earnings, with paid AI licensing of their lyrics to come
candidates.what_happened: Musixmatch relaunched Pro for Artists on 25 November 2026 with a Wallet that tracks what artists earn from their lyrics, lyric merchandise they can sell to fans, and engagement analytics. The Bologna company says more than 1.5 million artists use it, and that an optional setting will let them earn when AI platforms license their lyrics.
candidates.named_thing: Musixmatch Pro for Artists Wallet, optional AI lyric licensing

primary.label: Music Business Worldwide, 'Musixmatch launches enhanced Pro for Artists platform...with optional AI licensing coming soon', 25 Nov 2026
primary.quote: Musixmatch says optional AI licensing is 'coming soon' to the Wallet, giving artists an additional opportunity to earn from the authorized use of their lyrics by AI platforms.

more_sources.label: Music Business Worldwide, same article
more_sources.quote: The Bologna-based company says Musixmatch Pro for Artists is now used by more than 1.5 million artists.

candidates.money_or_mechanism: Musixmatch already holds licences to more than 15 million works from the three majors' publishers; the Wallet is where an artist's lyric merch sales and, later, AI licensing fees land.
candidates.why_it_matters: Songwriters get a named place to be paid when an AI service uses their words, run by the company that already supplies lyrics to the big streaming apps.
candidates.funny: The lyrics you misheard for years are about to have a licensing department.

helps.who: songwriters and artists who own their lyrics

candidates.risks: The AI licensing part is announced as 'coming soon' with no launch date and no AI platforms named; the merch Wallet is live. Company claim only. The picture on the MBW page may be a stock report graphic, not the product. Music Ally's version of this story was dropped by the first reader for its paywall; this is the open MBW report.

candidates.headline: Der Spiegel built a model that spots which subscribers are about to cancel, and it finds a third of them
candidates.what_happened: Der Spiegel's lead data scientist, Alexander Held, published how the German news magazine built a machine-learning score for subscriber churn, in a WAN-IFRA piece on 23 November 2026. The riskiest group it flags, close to 10,000 subscriptions, cancels at 28% against a base rate of about 4%, and that group holds about 36% of everyone who leaves.

primary.label: WAN-IFRA, 'Addressing subscriber churn at Der Spiegel, part one: building the score', Alexander Held, 23 Nov 2026
primary.quote: That came close to 10,000 subscriptions and they churn at 28% against a base rate of around 4%, seven times as high.

more_sources.label: WAN-IFRA, same article
more_sources.quote: It holds about 36% of everyone who leaves.

more_sources.label: WAN-IFRA, same article
more_sources.quote: subscriptions in their first 30 days leave at around 30%, those older than a year at 2.3%.

candidates.money_or_mechanism: The score lets the newsroom spend its retention offers on the tenth of readers who carry half of all cancellations instead of on everyone.
candidates.why_it_matters: A news publisher can now see a cancellation coming and act before the reader goes, which is subscription money kept.
candidates.funny: Spiegel built a model that can tell you are about to leave before you have opened the cancel page.
candidates.risks: Written by Spiegel's own data lead, so a first-person account. Part one only: how many subscribers the score actually saved is promised for part two. Machine learning rather than generative AI. The only real image on the page is the author's portrait; the lead photo is a placeholder.

candidates.headline: Nine is letting paying companies plug the AFR and the Sydney Morning Herald straight into their AI tools
candidates.what_happened: Australian publisher Nine announced on 25 November 2026 a pilot that lets licensed business subscribers connect its journalism from The Australian Financial Review, The Sydney Morning Herald, The Age, Brisbane Times and WAtoday to their own AI tools through the Model Context Protocol. It is testing with a group of business clients before a wider commercial rollout through 2027.

primary.label: Nine for Brands, 'Nine Leads With First-of-Its-Kind Authenticated MCP Publishing AI Pilot in Australia', 25 Nov 2026
primary.quote: allowing licensed B2B subscribers to securely authenticate and integrate Nine's trusted journalism

more_sources.label: Nine for Brands, same release
more_sources.quote: Nine's MCP recognises licensed B2B subscribers within their own secure enterprise environments.

candidates.money_or_mechanism: Instead of AI companies scraping the articles, the business that already pays for a subscription gets the reporting inside its own AI assistant, so the publisher keeps the customer and the fee.
candidates.why_it_matters: A newspaper group found a way to sell its journalism to AI users without giving it away to the AI companies.
candidates.funny: The newspaper's newest reader is a corporate chatbot, and it still has to log in.
candidates.risks: Company release only; no subscriber numbers, prices or revenue given. Pilot, with the commercial rollout set for 2027. The release page had no usable image. Also covered by iTnews and Mediaweek (24 to 25 Nov), not opened.

candidates.headline: An AI filmmaker made a fantasy comedy with a giant war beast for $28,775
candidates.what_happened: AI filmmaker PJ Ace (@pjacefilms) released a fantasy comedy about an Imperial army that recruits a wild warrior with a gigantic war beast who keeps destroying his own side. Evolving AI shared it on 31 October 2026 and said the whole film cost $28,775.

primary.label: Instagram, @evolving.ai post crediting @pjacefilms, 31 Oct 2026
primary.quote: Made for $28,775 total, the film features impressive animation, detailed fantasy worlds, expressive characters, and surprisingly good comedic timing.

more_sources.label: Instagram, same post
more_sources.quote: That’s the premise of this AI-generated fantasy comedy by @pjacefilms, where an Imperial army recruits a wildly unpredictable savage who commands a gigantic war beast capable of wiping out entire armies.

candidates.money_or_mechanism: A full fantasy short with creatures, armies and worlds came in under $30,000, a fraction of what the same effects would cost on a set.

candidates.funny: The army's biggest weapon keeps flattening its own side, which is the plot and also the history of most army procurement.

candidates.what_happened: Creator @tupacabra_og released 'Nuremberg', an AI-made trailer for an alternate-history epic mixing the Second World War, time travel, medieval Europe and future warfare, set to a 1903 recording of Kipling's poem 'Boots'. Evolving AI shared it on 14 November 2026, saying the visuals look like they belong in a $200 million Hollywood production.

primary.label: Instagram, @evolving.ai post crediting @tupacabra_og, 14 Nov 2026
primary.quote: From massive warships hovering over ancient cities to armies fighting across centuries, the visuals look like they belong in a $200 million Hollywood production.

more_sources.label: Instagram, same post
more_sources.quote: Created by @tupacabra_og, “Nuremberg” might be one of the most impressive AI-generated movie trailers we've seen yet.

candidates.money_or_mechanism: A one-person trailer reaches for the look of a nine-figure production, which is a pitch tool for a film nobody has had to fund yet.
candidates.why_it_matters: A creator can now show a studio what the film would look like before anyone pays for it.
candidates.funny: The soundtrack is a poem from 1903, which makes it the oldest thing in a trailer about time travel.
candidates.risks: The $200 million is the account's comparison, not a cost; no budget or views given. The caption also says 'Hollywood is about to get into serious trouble', a forecast we must not repeat. The title 'Nuremberg' may invite confusion with the 2025 courtroom film.
